{{ElectionsKS}}
The '''2026 Kansas gubernatorial election''' is scheduled to take place on November 3, 2026, to elect the next [[List of governors of Kansas|governor of Kansas]]. The primary elections took place on August 4, 2026.<ref>{{Cite web|date=May 9, 2025 |title=2026 State Primary Election Dates |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|publisher=NCSL |access-date=August 5, 2025}}</ref> Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Laura Kelly]] is term-limited and ineligible to seek a third consecutive term. This will be one of five Democratic-held governorships up for election in 2026 in a state that [[Donald Trump]] won in the [[2024 United States presidential election|2024 presidential election]] and the only one of those states that Trump won by a double-digit margin.

==Background==
Kansas has a long tradition of ticket-splitting at the gubernatorial level: despite the state's consistent support for Republican presidential nominees, Democratic candidates have won the governor's office for the majority of years since the late 1960s, reflecting a pattern of voters distinguishing between state executive and federal races.

This competitive tradition continued in the [[2018 Kansas gubernatorial election|2018 election]], when Laura Kelly won the open seat in a favorable national environment during the [[2018 United States elections|2018 midterms]] and benefited from widespread dissatisfaction with the outgoing administration of [[Sam Brownback]], who had departed mid-term after being nominated by President [[Donald Trump]] to serve as [[United States Ambassador-at-Large for International Religious Freedom]] in 2017.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Paul |first=Kari |date=November 7, 2018 |title=Kansas sees its own blue wave: 'If you can flip it here, you can flip it anywhere' |url=https://www.marketwatch.com/story/kansas-sees-its-own-blue-wave-if-you-can-flip-it-here-you-can-flip-it-anywhere-2018-11-07 |access-date=September 29, 2024 |work=[[MarketWatch]]}}</ref> Kelly won re-election in [[2022 Kansas gubernatorial election|2022]] on the strength of her own personal popularity, with the negative reaction to the [[Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization|overturning of ''Roe v. Wade'']] providing additional tailwind, amplified by the presence of an [[2022 Kansas abortion referendum|abortion referendum]] on the ballot a few months prior.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bahl |first=Andrew |title=National poll: More than half of residents approve of Gov. Laura Kelly's job performance |url=https://www.cjonline.com/story/news/politics/elections/2021/11/18/kansas-governor-laura-kelly-approval-rating-ahead-reelection-run-poll/8665879002/ |access-date=September 29, 2024 |website=[[The Topeka Capital-Journal]] |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Hanna |first=John |date=November 9, 2022 |title=Abortion rights support helps Kansas Gov. Kelly win 2nd term |url=https://apnews.com/article/2022-midterm-elections-biden-donald-trump-kansas-topeka-39afdff811fd2f30a212036d5ec6e3fa |access-date=September 29, 2024 |publisher=[[Associated Press]] |language=en}}</ref>

Since her re-election, Kelly has seen a continued rise in personal popularity, and as of 2024 ranks among the ten most popular governors in the country, which some commentators have attributed to her frequent use of her veto powers and extensive travel across the state.<ref>{{Cite web |date=April 23, 2024 |title=Report: Kansas gov. is one of the top 10 most popular in the nation |url=https://www.yahoo.com/news/report-kansas-gov-one-top-203024475.html |access-date=September 29, 2024 |website=[[Yahoo News]] |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |author=A. O. L. Staff |date=May 4, 2024 |title=Are Gov. Laura Kelly's rising approval numbers because of her frequent use of veto powers? |url=https://www.aol.com/gov-laura-kellys-rising-approval-090237691.html |access-date=September 29, 2024 |via=AOL news |language=en-US}}</ref>
While Democratic candidates have remained competitive at the gubernatorial level, the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]] has historically dominated Kansas in federal and legislative politics. After the [[2024 United States House of Representatives elections in Kansas|2024 elections]], Republicans maintained their 3-1 majority in Kansas's U.S. House delegation.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Mesa |first=Blaise |date=January 6, 2026 |title=Kansas Republicans don't have the votes for redistricting in 2026, house speaker says |url=https://www.kcur.org/politics-elections-and-government/2026-01-06/kansas-republicans-redistricting-congress-sharice-davids |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260107132748/https://www.kcur.org/politics-elections-and-government/2026-01-06/kansas-republicans-redistricting-congress-sharice-davids |archive-date=January 7, 2026 |access-date=January 16, 2026 |publisher=[[NPR]] Kansas City}}</ref> Kansas has been represented in the U.S. Senate exclusively by Republicans since 1939.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Rudin |first=Ken |date=December 8, 2008 |title=Longest Losing Streaks In The Senate |url=https://www.npr.org/sections/politicaljunkie/2008/12/longest_losing_streaks_in_the_1.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230412212226/https://www.npr.org/sections/politicaljunkie/2008/12/longest_losing_streaks_in_the_1.html |archive-date=April 12, 2023 |access-date=January 16, 2026 |publisher=[[NPR]]}}</ref> Both chambers of the [[Kansas Legislature]] also have Republican supermajorities.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Self |first=Matthew |date=December 3, 2024 |title=Kansas Republicans retain supermajority control in the state Legislature |url=https://www.ksnt.com/elections/kansas-republicans-retain-supermajority-control-in-the-state-legislature/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250127190450/https://www.ksnt.com/elections/kansas-republicans-retain-supermajority-control-in-the-state-legislature/ |archive-date=January 27, 2025 |access-date=January 16, 2026 |publisher=[[KSNT]] |location=Topeka}}</ref> Since 1957, neither major political party has held the Kansas governor's office for longer than two consecutive terms, reflecting the ongoing competitiveness of the state's executive elections.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ballotpedia - Kansas State Government |url=https://ballotpedia.org/Party_control_of_Kansas_state_government |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251102082632/https://ballotpedia.org/Party_control_of_Kansas_state_government |archive-date=November 2, 2025 |access-date=January 16, 2026 |website=[[Ballotpedia]]}}</ref>
